question: According to a recent OXFAM press release, European billionaires increased their wealth by over EUR 400 billion in the first half of 2025. This is a record high, with the creation of a new European billionaire reported every 9 days in the last year – and this at a time when, according to Eurostat data, one in five Europeans (21 %) is facing poverty and social exclusion.

According to the research data, the richest 1 % of Europeans own almost 25 % of all wealth, while the poorest half of the population own only 3 %. The cost-of-living crisis has eroded wages, while governments are diverting funds away from public services and into defence.
At the same time, European citizens are footing the bill, with 80 % of tax revenue in the EU coming from taxes mostly incurred by ordinary citizens. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it intend to take this report into consideration?

If so, what measures could it take to tax the super-rich and to address the lack of harmonisation that fuels aggressive tax competition and allows them to exploit legislative loopholes and minimise their tax contribution?
answer: The Commission takes note of the report from Oxfam (1). The Commission launched in December 2024 a study on wealth-related taxes to have a better understanding of the effective taxation of high-net-worth individuals. It is foreseen to be completed in the first half of 2026.

It will provide further information on the overall context and on the effectiveness of wealth-related taxes targeting high-net-worth-individuals in both EU and non-EU countries. Moreover, to have better insights, the Commission can build on the EUROMOD (2) microsimulation tool, i.e. the EU taxbenefit microsimulation model. This tool estimates the effects of changes in taxes and benefits on household income.
It also assesses work-related incentives across the population of each country and for the EU as a whole. The Commission has taken several actions to achieve fairer outcomes.

A major achievement aimed at curbing tax avoidance and evasion is the directive on the Administrative Cooperation (3) and its numerous updates that improve transparency, administrative cooperation and exchange of information between Member States as well as the European Semester Country specific recommendations (4) on aggressive tax planning.
